Here is an English translation of this Sumerian text (likely from a mythological or liturgical composition concerning Inanna):

1. In those days of old, when heaven and earth had been [fashioned together],
2. In those nights of old, when heaven and earth had been [fashioned together],
3. In those [years] of old, when destinies had been [decreed],
4. When the Anunnaki had been born,
5. When Inanna had attained lordship/authority,
6. When Inanna had spread herself across heaven and earth,
7. When Inanna [...] had grown great and given birth,
8. The gods of the inspection, their A X X, were bound toward their dining hall,
9. The great gods stood at their tasks; the lesser gods were carrying the toil and burden,
10. The gods were digging the rivers and canals, piling up their silt,
11. The gods were complaining; their spirits were setting down their words,
12. In those days, the broad wisdom of the blood of all the great gods existed —
13. Enki, in the deep abyss, in the underground waters, a place no god could marvel at,
14. In his bedchamber he lay, he would not rise from sleep,
15. The gods were weeping and lamenting, making mourning,
16. To the one who lay sleeping, their sleeping place would not let him rise,
17. Namma, the primeval mother who gave birth to all the great gods,
18. Brought the tears of the gods to her son,
19. "X, he lay there sleeping, he lay there slumbering" —
20. [X] TE BA [...he would] not rise,
21. "The god of your handiwork, X, are consuming his/its neck/voice."

---

**Notes on the translation:**

- This text shares close parallels with the **Eridu Genesis** and mythological texts related to **Enki and Namma** (the creation of humanity), likely from the Old Babylonian period.
- Lines 9–11 reflect the motif of the gods laboring before humanity's creation, paralleling the **Atrahasis Epic**.
- Several signs are damaged or ambiguous (marked with X, brackets, or question marks in the original), so those passages are rendered tentatively.
- Line 13's reference to Enki sleeping in the **engur** (the primordial underground freshwater abyss) is a classic mythological motif.
- The text likely leads toward the creation of humans to relieve the gods of their labor.
